rv.q: What lingers, in the end, is the uncomfortable recognition that the characters’ hubris is not entirely alien.
Buttressed by big ideas and gripping performances, Spare Parts is both livelier and more entertaining than his previous play.
His concerns are real; his story is silly.
In an era when new plays often struggle to find both intellectual rigor and theatrical propulsion, Spare Parts manages to deliver both.
The dramatic twists of the play's conclusion do somewhat strain the nuanced drama set up by its first hour.
The ending is quite good, in a shocking "oh, they went there!" kind of way, which director Michael Herwitz handles with a sure hand.
It is a win-lose scenario, effectively anchoring the goings-on in believability while simultaneously dragging down the action.

cn.t: Critics praise "Spare Parts" for its provocative exploration of mortality and hubris, with playwright David J. Glass's biomedical expertise lending authenticity to this timely sci-fi drama about a tech billionaire's quest to cheat aging.

vr.q: Spare Parts is a thought-provoking, sharply acted, smartly directed new play that is asking exactly the right questions for this moment in time.
the play ends up feeling stiff and too contrived to meaningfully engage with the ethical dilemmas it intends to invoke
